analysis.one_liner: Wipes out federal regulators' climate-risk guidance for large banks and bars similar rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it got two cosponsors and no vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2023 the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC jointly issued guidance telling very large banks to plan for climate-related financial risks, such as loan losses from floods, wildfires, or the economy's shift away from carbon. This bill would erase that guidance and forbid the agencies from issuing anything substantially like it again. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest financial institutions would gain: they would no longer face supervisory expectations to incorporate climate-related financial risk into their strategic planning, governance, and risk management [S2]. Industries whose financing depends on bank lending decisions, such as carbon-intensive energy projects, would also face less pressure from lenders assessing transition risk [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the October 2023 interagency guidance 'Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management for Large Financial Institutions' has no force or effect, and that the Fed, OCC, and FDIC may not issue substantially similar guidance [S2].
That guidance applies to large financial institutions, so its removal would spare those institutions the supervisory expectations it set [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary savers, depositors, and ultimately taxpayers bear more risk if large banks are less prepared for climate-related losses, since the federal safety net absorbs bank failures. Communities exposed to climate-driven shocks also lose an early-warning mechanism in the financial system [S2].

drawbacks.text: Removing the guidance would leave bank supervisors without their stated framework for ensuring large institutions manage climate-related financial risk, including physical risks like disasters and transition risks as the economy decarbonizes [S2].

Banking industry objections in good faith: the agencies issued this as guidance rather than through formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which critics argued bypassed required process, and they argued it could push banks to retreat from lending to legal energy businesses; the bill's response was to nullify the guidance outright rather than re-issue it through rulemaking [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows to a narrow set of very large banks, while the cost is diffuse and deferred: weaker preparation across the financial system for climate-related losses, which in a downturn or disaster would fall on depositors and taxpayers through the federal safety net. A fairer approach to the banks' procedural objection would have been re-issuing expectations through formal rulemaking, not erasing them entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 14, 2024, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 14, 2024 by Representative Troy Balderson of Ohio, joined by two cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].

It targeted the final interagency guidance published October 24, 2023 by the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC, titled 'Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management for Large Financial Institutions' [S2].

The House action history shows only two entries: introduction and referral to the Committee on Financial Services, with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended [S4].
Because the bill never became law, the guidance it sought to nullify was never removed, and the agencies' climate-risk expectations for large institutions remained in place [S2][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the regulators' climate-risk guidance for large banks stayed on the books, and the large financial institutions that wanted it erased did not get their way [S2][S4].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators' guidance stands; banks gain nothing

for.name: Troy Balderson
for.role: U.S. Representative, Ohio's 12th district; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the interagency climate-risk guidance [S1][S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill received no committee action after its referral [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Republicans, no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill's only two cosponsors came from a caucus of 224 House Republicans [S3].

industries.note: The bill would have freed them from the Fed, OCC, and FDIC's 2023 supervisory expectations to manage climate-related financial risk [S2]. Their gain is the public's loss of an early-warning framework, since losses banks fail to prepare for fall back on depositors and the federal safety net.

With banks no longer directed to weigh climate transition risk in lending, financing for fossil-heavy projects would face less supervisory pressure from lenders [S2]. The benefit is indirect but flows from the same removal of oversight.
